messages.subject: Convergence problems for state-space time-series model
parts:
Hi All,

I'm trying to build a Nimble model for count-based time-series that contain autocorrelation. Essentially, it's supposed to look like this:

y_t ~ Pois(lambda_t)
lambda_t <- lambda_t-1 * exp(eta + B0 + XB)
eta ~ N(0,sd_eta)
B ~ multivariateN(0,sd_beta)

y_t = count at time t
lambda_t = process mean at t
lambda_t-1 = process mean at t-1
eta = stochastic shock
X = covariate matrix
B0 = intercept

My primary interest is in estimating B0 and B so I can compare models with different sets of covariates. I use the attached scripts in R to generate simulated time-series and the relevant Nimble code. Just run pois_data.R and then nimble_pois.R to reproduce what I'm seeing.

I've only just started learning state-space modelling, Bayes, and MCMC. So, I'm not sure if the model is impossible to estimate accurately or if there's something I could be doing differently with the MCMC to reach convergence. I have had some luck with convergence when using strong priors on B0 and eta, but long MCMC runs (1000000 iterations) still eventually go for a random walk. Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Convergence problems for state-space time-series model
parts:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for the query.  When I ran your data simulation code,  simdata_counts turned out to be all zeros.  This seems to have created a pathological case for parameter estimation.  The posteriors are to a first glance reasonably mixed, but the B0 values are very negative and some of the other dimensions are sampling a huge range (maybe essentially their priors).  When I add up the terms in the exponent that appears for lambda[j] to get a posterior sample of that exponent for each time step, I get largely very negative values.  So it seems that the posterior is saying there is essentially no information in the data except that lambdas should be zero because the Ys are all zero.  I presume you'll want to try things out with more interesting simulated data, or let me know if I've done something wrong.

A couple of other notes on your model:

Having lambda0 follow a gamma that is mixed over uniform parameters might be excessive.

The random effects eta[j] ("process noise") typically have a std. deviation that is a parameter to be estimated, not fixed at something large.  As written, it's like saying you are sure that extrinsic bumps to the system are of enormous scale rather than estimating the scale of their distribution.

Finally, making eta[j] follow a normal and then inserting it into the deterministic node for lambda[j] creates an inefficient graph.  It means that if eta[j] is sampled in the MCMC, then  *all* of lambda[j]...lambda[T] and the Poisson log probabilities of Y[j]...Y[T] must be calculated, either to accept/reject and/or to update the state of the model.  As T gets big, this does not scale well.

If instead you write

for(j in 2:T) {
loglambda[j] ~ dnorm(loglambda[j-1] + B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]), sd = 1000) ## except that "1000" should be a parameter as noted above, but I just wrote it as you had in your code.
}
for(j in 1:T) {
Y[j] ~ dpois(exp(loglambda[j]))
}

then you will have a more efficient graph.  There is no eta[j], but loglambda[j] is stochastic.  If loglambda[j] is sampled in the MCMC, only the log probabilities of loglambda[j], loglambda[j+1] and Y[j] must be calculated.

Perry

parts:
Hi Chris,

I see several thing going on.

Perhaps most importantly, you have not included samplers for the lambda[j]s.  You can add 'lambda' to the nodes argument to configureMCMC.  Alternatively, I typically omit the nodes argument, which means all non-data stochastic nodes will be sampled, which means I won't forget something by accident.  If you want to customize samplers (as it looks like you do), you can then remove samplers for 'a' and 'b' (poisTSModel_conf$removeSamplers(c('a','b'); poisTSModel_conf$printSamplers() to inspect what you have) before adding the new sampler(s). 

It looks like you've accidentally placed a highly informative prior on B0.  I think you want 
B0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
Without the "sd = ", it will treat 1000 as a precision, so sd = 0.01, effectively assuming B0 must be nearly 0.

It looks like your use of dmnorm is not quite what you want.  The way to interpret the entries in Table 5.2 of the user manual is that you could use either

B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], cholesky=cholA[1:K,1:K], prec_param = 1)
or
B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], prec=A[1:K,1:K]) ## don't need cholA in this case; nimble will calculate it as a "lifted node"

Your code says that cholA is the precision matrix, which I don't think is what you want.

I'm still not sure you have much information on the impact of X is in the simulated time-series.  When I compared a Poisson-normal mixture using the std.dev. of 0.001 to the simulated Y values, it looked fairly consistent.  And I see that the B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]) values in the simulation are all very small.  So the Poisson observation error might somewhat swamp the signal in this case, and the estimates might essentially say there are no interesting dynamics, but you'll have to see once you have the model fixed.  It is not uncommon in state-space models to have a hard time separating process noise from observation error for a particular time series.

I don't know the domain context of your model.  It looks like the kind of model people use for population dynamics, where lambda[j] is a latent population density and the lambda dynamics are multiplicative because that's how populations change.  In that case, people typically add process noise on a log scale (i.e., in the exponent) to represent "environmental stochasticity".  If reproduction is high (or mortality is low) due to random conditions in one year, those rates affect the whole population, which corresponds to a random variation on the log scale.  If you add noise on the non-log scale, but with standard deviation that does not vary with time (as you have done in the current code), then effectively you are saying that process noise has a smaller relative impact when lambda is large and a larger relative impact when lambda is small.  That may not correspond to the concepts the model should represent.

If results still don't seem to make sense, you might try providing initial values for the lambda.  In some cases this can be very helpful.  For example, you could set initial lambda to equal Y plus some jitter (or log(Y) + jitter for loglambda, if you switch to the log scale).

Perry

I'm glad to hear things are coming together.

To avoid the inefficient graph, you need to have the latent states themselves be stochastic, so that there is conditional independence through the time-series or latent states.  The loglambda version I suggested previously would do that.  I think the modification from your latest code would be:

for (j in 2:T){
      mu[j] <- inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K])
      loglambda[j] ~ dnorm( loglambda[j-1] + mu[j], sd = stdev)
      lambda[j] <- exp(loglambda[j])
   }

Now loglambda[j] depends on loglambda[j-1] but is conditionally independent from loglambda[j-2] etc.

The model is mathematically equivalent to your code, but the latent states themselves rather than the process noises are written as stochastic.

Perry

On Fri, Oct 13, 2017 at 1:41 PM, Chris Carleton <w.cca...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Perry,

I just looked at a Cor(samples)[B[1],lambdas] and saw only low correlations (near zero, centered on zero overall). So, maybe it's something that only happens for specific simulated data. On Oct 13, 2017 11:48 AM, "Perry de Valpine" <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
Now the temporal dynamics of lambda are a non-stationary random walk.  That can often cause problems in estimation and may not be what you really want.  In this case, the intercept (B[1]) and all of the lambda[j]s are all very highly correlated with each other.  Try cor(samples) and make some pairwise plots to see that.  They seem to be nearly non-identifiable.  A small increase in B[1] can be compensated by the same small decrease in all lambda[j]s, which leaves the probabilities unchanged except for lambda[1].  That means B[1] cannot practically be separated from the lambda[j]s in much of a meaningful way.  It's common to make the dynamics of the (log of the) latent state auto-regressive and anticipate estimates of the auto-correlation between -1 and 1, but only you can say if that makes sense for your problem.

Also your data simulations are extremely variable.  If I run it several times, I sometimes get count series with explosions over many orders of magnitude, and sometimes just mild fluctuations.

The MCMC reaches (correct) convergence for the other covariates and parameters, but not the intercept. I've tried modelling the intercept separately as in B0 + XB and as a column of 1s in the X matrix with the same results—i.e., no convergence on an estimate of the intercept even after 2000000 iterations. Oddly, I can leave the intercept out altogether and replace the relevant column in the X matrix with another random covariate and the MCMC will happily converge for all covariates. I've attached the code again and if you or anyone else has some time to look over it, I'd really appreciate it. 

Many thanks,

Chris

On Tuesday, October 10, 2017 at 3:53:43 PM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
I'm glad to hear things are coming together.

To avoid the inefficient graph, you need to have the latent states themselves be stochastic, so that there is conditional independence through the time-series or latent states.  The loglambda version I suggested previously would do that.  I think the modification from your latest code would be:

for (j in 2:T){
      mu[j] <- inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K])
      loglambda[j] ~ dnorm( loglambda[j-1] + mu[j], sd = stdev)
      lambda[j] <- exp(loglambda[j])
   }

Now loglambda[j] depends on loglambda[j-1] but is conditionally independent from loglambda[j-2] etc.

The model is mathematically equivalent to your code, but the latent states themselves rather than the process noises are written as stochastic.

Perry

On Friday, October 6, 2017 at 9:50:55 AM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
Hi Chris,

I see several thing going on.

Perhaps most importantly, you have not included samplers for the lambda[j]s.  You can add 'lambda' to the nodes argument to configureMCMC.  Alternatively, I typically omit the nodes argument, which means all non-data stochastic nodes will be sampled, which means I won't forget something by accident.  If you want to customize samplers (as it looks like you do), you can then remove samplers for 'a' and 'b' (poisTSModel_conf$removeSamplers(c('a','b'); poisTSModel_conf$printSamplers() to inspect what you have) before adding the new sampler(s). 

It looks like you've accidentally placed a highly informative prior on B0.  I think you want 
B0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
Without the "sd = ", it will treat 1000 as a precision, so sd = 0.01, effectively assuming B0 must be nearly 0.

It looks like your use of dmnorm is not quite what you want.  The way to interpret the entries in Table 5.2 of the user manual is that you could use either

B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], cholesky=cholA[1:K,1:K], prec_param = 1)
or
B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], prec=A[1:K,1:K]) ## don't need cholA in this case; nimble will calculate it as a "lifted node"

Your code says that cholA is the precision matrix, which I don't think is what you want.

I'm still not sure you have much information on the impact of X is in the simulated time-series.  When I compared a Poisson-normal mixture using the std.dev. of 0.001 to the simulated Y values, it looked fairly consistent.  And I see that the B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]) values in the simulation are all very small.  So the Poisson observation error might somewhat swamp the signal in this case, and the estimates might essentially say there are no interesting dynamics, but you'll have to see once you have the model fixed.  It is not uncommon in state-space models to have a hard time separating process noise from observation error for a particular time series.

I don't know the domain context of your model.  It looks like the kind of model people use for population dynamics, where lambda[j] is a latent population density and the lambda dynamics are multiplicative because that's how populations change.  In that case, people typically add process noise on a log scale (i.e., in the exponent) to represent "environmental stochasticity".  If reproduction is high (or mortality is low) due to random conditions in one year, those rates affect the whole population, which corresponds to a random variation on the log scale.  If you add noise on the non-log scale, but with standard deviation that does not vary with time (as you have done in the current code), then effectively you are saying that process noise has a smaller relative impact when lambda is large and a larger relative impact when lambda is small.  That may not correspond to the concepts the model should represent.

If results still don't seem to make sense, you might try providing initial values for the lambda.  In some cases this can be very helpful.  For example, you could set initial lambda to equal Y plus some jitter (or log(Y) + jitter for loglambda, if you switch to the log scale).

Perry

On Thursday, October 5, 2017 at 3:12:38 PM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for the query.  When I ran your data simulation code,  simdata_counts turned out to be all zeros.  This seems to have created a pathological case for parameter estimation.  The posteriors are to a first glance reasonably mixed, but the B0 values are very negative and some of the other dimensions are sampling a huge range (maybe essentially their priors).  When I add up the terms in the exponent that appears for lambda[j] to get a posterior sample of that exponent for each time step, I get largely very negative values.  So it seems that the posterior is saying there is essentially no information in the data except that lambdas should be zero because the Ys are all zero.  I presume you'll want to try things out with more interesting simulated data, or let me know if I've done something wrong.

A couple of other notes on your model:

Having lambda0 follow a gamma that is mixed over uniform parameters might be excessive.

The random effects eta[j] ("process noise") typically have a std. deviation that is a parameter to be estimated, not fixed at something large.  As written, it's like saying you are sure that extrinsic bumps to the system are of enormous scale rather than estimating the scale of their distribution.

Finally, making eta[j] follow a normal and then inserting it into the deterministic node for lambda[j] creates an inefficient graph.  It means that if eta[j] is sampled in the MCMC, then  *all* of lambda[j]...lambda[T] and the Poisson log probabilities of Y[j]...Y[T] must be calculated, either to accept/reject and/or to update the state of the model.  As T gets big, this does not scale well.

If instead you write

for(j in 2:T) {
loglambda[j] ~ dnorm(loglambda[j-1] + B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]), sd = 1000) ## except that "1000" should be a parameter as noted above, but I just wrote it as you had in your code.
}
for(j in 1:T) {
Y[j] ~ dpois(exp(loglambda[j]))
}

then you will have a more efficient graph.  There is no eta[j], but loglambda[j] is stochastic.  If loglambda[j] is sampled in the MCMC, only the log probabilities of loglambda[j], loglambda[j+1] and Y[j] must be calculated.

Perry

On Thu, Oct 5, 2017 at 2:22 PM, Chris Carleton <w.cca...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi All,

I'm trying to build a Nimble model for count-based time-series that contain autocorrelation. Essentially, it's supposed to look like this:

y_t ~ Pois(lambda_t)
lambda_t <- lambda_t-1 * exp(eta + B0 + XB)
eta ~ N(0,sd_eta)
B ~ multivariateN(0,sd_beta)

y_t = count at time t
lambda_t = process mean at t
lambda_t-1 = process mean at t-1
eta = stochastic shock
X = covariate matrix
B0 = intercept

My primary interest is in estimating B0 and B so I can compare models with different sets of covariates. I use the attached scripts in R to generate simulated time-series and the relevant Nimble code. Just run pois_data.R and then nimble_pois.R to reproduce what I'm seeing.

I've only just started learning state-space modelling, Bayes, and MCMC. So, I'm not sure if the model is impossible to estimate accurately or if there's something I could be doing differently with the MCMC to reach convergence. I have had some luck with convergence when using strong priors on B0 and eta, but long MCMC runs (1000000 iterations) still eventually go for a random walk. Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Chris

To avoid the inefficient graph, you need to have the latent states themselves be stochastic, so that there is conditional independence through the time-series or latent states.  The loglambda version I suggested previously would do that.  I think the modification from your latest code would be:

Hi Chris,

I see several thing going on.

Perhaps most importantly, you have not included samplers for the lambda[j]s.  You can add 'lambda' to the nodes argument to configureMCMC.  Alternatively, I typically omit the nodes argument, which means all non-data stochastic nodes will be sampled, which means I won't forget something by accident.  If you want to customize samplers (as it looks like you do), you can then remove samplers for 'a' and 'b' (poisTSModel_conf$removeSamplers(c('a','b'); poisTSModel_conf$printSamplers() to inspect what you have) before adding the new sampler(s). 

It looks like you've accidentally placed a highly informative prior on B0.  I think you want 
B0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
Without the "sd = ", it will treat 1000 as a precision, so sd = 0.01, effectively assuming B0 must be nearly 0.

It looks like your use of dmnorm is not quite what you want.  The way to interpret the entries in Table 5.2 of the user manual is that you could use either

B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], cholesky=cholA[1:K,1:K], prec_param = 1)
or
B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], prec=A[1:K,1:K]) ## don't need cholA in this case; nimble will calculate it as a "lifted node"

Your code says that cholA is the precision matrix, which I don't think is what you want.

I'm still not sure you have much information on the impact of X is in the simulated time-series.  When I compared a Poisson-normal mixture using the std.dev. of 0.001 to the simulated Y values, it looked fairly consistent.  And I see that the B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]) values in the simulation are all very small.  So the Poisson observation error might somewhat swamp the signal in this case, and the estimates might essentially say there are no interesting dynamics, but you'll have to see once you have the model fixed.  It is not uncommon in state-space models to have a hard time separating process noise from observation error for a particular time series.

I don't know the domain context of your model.  It looks like the kind of model people use for population dynamics, where lambda[j] is a latent population density and the lambda dynamics are multiplicative because that's how populations change.  In that case, people typically add process noise on a log scale (i.e., in the exponent) to represent "environmental stochasticity".  If reproduction is high (or mortality is low) due to random conditions in one year, those rates affect the whole population, which corresponds to a random variation on the log scale.  If you add noise on the non-log scale, but with standard deviation that does not vary with time (as you have done in the current code), then effectively you are saying that process noise has a smaller relative impact when lambda is large and a larger relative impact when lambda is small.  That may not correspond to the concepts the model should represent.

If results still don't seem to make sense, you might try providing initial values for the lambda.  In some cases this can be very helpful.  For example, you could set initial lambda to equal Y plus some jitter (or log(Y) + jitter for loglambda, if you switch to the log scale).

Hi Chris,

Thanks for the query.  When I ran your data simulation code,  simdata_counts turned out to be all zeros.  This seems to have created a pathological case for parameter estimation.  The posteriors are to a first glance reasonably mixed, but the B0 values are very negative and some of the other dimensions are sampling a huge range (maybe essentially their priors).  When I add up the terms in the exponent that appears for lambda[j] to get a posterior sample of that exponent for each time step, I get largely very negative values.  So it seems that the posterior is saying there is essentially no information in the data except that lambdas should be zero because the Ys are all zero.  I presume you'll want to try things out with more interesting simulated data, or let me know if I've done something wrong.

A couple of other notes on your model:

Having lambda0 follow a gamma that is mixed over uniform parameters might be excessive.

The random effects eta[j] ("process noise") typically have a std. deviation that is a parameter to be estimated, not fixed at something large.  As written, it's like saying you are sure that extrinsic bumps to the system are of enormous scale rather than estimating the scale of their distribution.

Finally, making eta[j] follow a normal and then inserting it into the deterministic node for lambda[j] creates an inefficient graph.  It means that if eta[j] is sampled in the MCMC, then  *all* of lambda[j]...lambda[T] and the Poisson log probabilities of Y[j]...Y[T] must be calculated, either to accept/reject and/or to update the state of the model.  As T gets big, this does not scale well.

If instead you write

for(j in 2:T) {
loglambda[j] ~ dnorm(loglambda[j-1] + B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]), sd = 1000) ## except that "1000" should be a parameter as noted above, but I just wrote it as you had in your code.
}
for(j in 1:T) {
Y[j] ~ dpois(exp(loglambda[j]))
}

then you will have a more efficient graph.  There is no eta[j], but loglambda[j] is stochastic.  If loglambda[j] is sampled in the MCMC, only the log probabilities of loglambda[j], loglambda[j+1] and Y[j] must be calculated.

Perry
